meta.subtitle: Levered aluminum converter with strong 2026 earnings, a consensus step-down into FY27 and $1.8B of net debt behind a deep bear case

analystCommentary: We rate Constellium a HOLD with a $21 to $27 target range against the September 29, 2026 price of $24.59. Our probability-weighted fair value is $25.22, an expected upside of 2.6%, against a bear-case downside of 41.5%, for a reward/risk of 0.06x. The shares look cheap on trailing earnings, and the aerospace business is growing. The price looks less generous against next year: consensus EPS steps down from $3.66 in FY26E to $2.41 in FY27E, and the shares already trade at 10.2x that lower figure. The company also carries substantial net debt, which is more than half the market value of its equity, so a shortfall in earnings would fall harder on the shares than on the business. That debt is why our Bear is deep and why the reward/risk sits far below what a BUY needs.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Constellium makes rolled and extruded aluminum products for the aerospace, space, defense, packaging, automotive, commercial transportation and general industrial end-markets. It was incorporated in 2010 and is headquartered in Paris, France. At June 30, 2026 it operated 23 manufacturing facilities with approximately 11,500 employees, with operations in the United States, France, Germany, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Mexico and Canada. The 10-Q reports three operating segments: Aerospace & Transportation, Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products, and Automotive Structures & Industry. FY25 revenue was $8.4 billion, up 15.2%, with net income of $273 million and diluted EPS of $1.92. It pays no dividend and returns cash through buybacks.

thesis.body: Constellium's earnings have risen sharply in 2026 on higher metal prices and a recovering aerospace business, and we think today's price already pays for the earnings consensus expects next year. Quarterly revenue growth has come from revenue per ton, while total shipments slipped. Consensus models EPS falling into FY27E, and the shares trade on that lower figure at about the multiple we use in our Base. The Bull needs FY27 earnings to hold near the FY26E level; the Bear needs them to fall back toward FY25's, and the debt carried on the balance sheet turns that into a deep loss for shareholders. We weight those two paths equally around a Base at today's price, which leaves a small expected upside against a large downside, so we rate the shares a HOLD.

catalysts: Aerospace: Aerospace & Transportation, the segment that earns the most per dollar of revenue, is the one segment growing volumes, and management says aerospace demand has improved.
A strong 2026: first-half net income already exceeds the FY25 total, which supports delivery of the FY26E consensus.
Buybacks: the company repurchased $115 million of stock in FY25 and another $20 million in Q2'26.
North American tightness: management credited Q2'26 partly to supply shortages of automotive rolled products in North America and to strong recycling performance.
risks: Earnings step-down: consensus EPS falls from $3.66 in FY26E to $2.41 in FY27E.
Leverage: FY25 net debt of $1.8 billion magnifies any fall in earnings for shareholders.
Volumes outside aerospace: Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products shipped fewer tons in Q2'26.
Trade policy: the 10-K warns that shifts in trade policy and tariffs could adversely affect results, and the Midwest premium rose 154% in Q2'26 after the Section 232 tariff announcements.
Energy: the 10-Q says the conflict in the Middle East has caused, and may continue to result in, higher fuel and energy prices.

financials.incomeCommentary: The pack carries no operating-income or EBITDA line, so this section works from the 10-Q statement. Q2'26 revenue rose {+ 31% +} year over year to $2,748 million from $2,103 million. The company attributes the increase to higher revenue per ton, including higher metal prices, partially offset by lower shipments. Volumes fell {- 1% -} to 381 kt: a 21% rise in Aerospace & Transportation was outweighed by a 4% decrease in Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products, with Automotive Structures & Industry stable. Cost of sales, excluding depreciation and amortization, was 83% of revenue against 87% a year earlier, and income before tax rose to $214 million from $56 million. Management credits the quarter to "strong operational focus, cost control and improved market dynamics", including the aerospace and defense environment, North American auto-sheet shortages and recycling. Net income was $148 million against $36 million, even though other gains and losses moved to a $39 million loss from a $4 million gain. First-half net income of $344 million already exceeds the FY25 full-year figure. The annual record shows how far earnings can swing: revenue fell in FY23 and FY24, and diluted EPS fell from $2.10 in FY22 to $0.38 in FY24 before recovering in FY25. We read 2026 as a strong year for a business whose earnings have proved volatile, not as a new base.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet carries real debt. Total debt was $1.9 billion at FY23, FY24 and FY25, and net debt was $1.8 billion at FY24 and FY25 after $1.7 billion at FY23. Cash and short-term investments were only $0.1 billion at FY25. Total equity rose to $1.0 billion at FY25 from $0.7 billion, so debt was still nearly twice equity. The pack has no EBITDA series, so it gives no net debt/EBITDA or interest-coverage ratio. The company's own measure, in the April 2026 proxy, is leverage of 2.5x at the end of 2025, alongside FY25 Adjusted EBITDA of $846 million, a non-GAAP figure; the excerpt does not define the ratio, and we cite it as the company's measure. Because net debt was flat from FY24 to FY25 on the pack's figures, the reduction in that ratio came from higher earnings rather than a smaller debt balance. Servicing looks comfortable for now: Q2'26 net finance costs were $28 million against $29 million a year earlier, a small charge next to the quarter's pre-tax income. The risk runs the other way. A ratio that fell because earnings rose will rise again if earnings fall back, and with net debt more than half the market value of the equity, shareholders carry that swing. The TTM current ratio of 1.43, up from 1.29 at FY25, points to adequate short-term liquidity.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is positive but thin. FY25 operating cash flow was about $0.5 billion and capital expenditure $330 million, leaving free cash flow of $159 million on the vendor's figures, a 1.9% FCF margin. The proxy reports $178 million of Free Cash Flow on the company's non-GAAP definition; the two sources disagree, and this report uses the vendor's figure. The record is uneven: the FCF margin was 0.9% in FY22 and 0.8% in FY23, and free cash flow was negative in FY24, at a -1.5% margin. The trailing FCF yield is 6.5%. The company pays no dividend. The structural point is that an aluminum roller must keep reinvesting in its plants, so even a strong revenue year leaves a small cash surplus against the debt described above.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing numbers the shares look cheap: 6.4x TTM earnings, 0.3x sales and 4.1x TTM EV/EBITDA. The forward picture is less cheap. The vendor labels its 6.7x forward multiple next-twelve-months, but it matches the FY26E consensus EPS of $3.66, so it is a current-year multiple. On the FY27E consensus EPS of $2.41 the multiple is 10.2x. The pack gives no reason for the consensus step-down. We value the shares on FY27E, because more than half of FY26 is already reported and the price has to rest on what comes after it. The trailing multiples are measured on earnings well above any full year in the four-year record, so they flatter the stock. With net debt large relative to the equity, the enterprise multiple is the fairer comparison than P/E, but the pack shows no EBITDA series to check that multiple against. No peer multiples are in the pack. The Street is constructive: 4 of 5 analysts rate the shares a Buy, with a $35.78 consensus target, a $35.91 median and a $33.05-$38.87 range. Our weighted fair value sits below the whole range because we price a Bear the Street targets do not reach.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: FY27 earnings hold near the FY26E consensus EPS of $3.66 instead of stepping down, as Aerospace & Transportation volumes keep rising and the North American auto-sheet and recycling conditions persist. The market keeps paying today's 10.2x FY27E multiple, now on FY26E-level EPS. Implied price $37.33, inside the $33.05-$38.87 analyst target range and just above the $36.99 52-week high.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus proves right: EPS steps down to the FY27E $2.41, aerospace growth offsets softer packaging and automotive volumes, and the shares keep today's FY27E multiple on that figure. Net debt stays near the FY25 level as free cash flow goes mainly to buybacks. Implied price $24.58, in line with the current price.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Earnings fall below consensus toward FY25's $1.92 diluted EPS as the conditions management credited for Q2'26, North American auto-sheet shortages and strong recycling performance, fade and packaging volumes keep slipping. With net debt unchanged, the lower earnings fall entirely on the equity, and the shares revisit their $14.39 52-week low, a price they traded at within the past year; that low is the implied price.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting the Bull at 25%, the Base at 50% and the Bear at 25% gives a weighted fair value of $25.22, an expected upside of 2.6%, a bear-case downside of 41.5% and a reward/risk of 0.06x, which derives HOLD. The deciding split is Bull against Bear. The case for more Bear weight is the FY22-to-FY24 earnings fall described in the income section, and the fact that the Bear needs a smaller miss against FY27E consensus than the Bull needs a beat. The case for more Bull weight is a strong first half and an aerospace business still growing volumes at double digits. We weight the two equally; that is a judgment, not a finding. The call sits closer to SELL than to BUY: moving less than ten points of weight from the Bull to the Bear derives SELL, while a BUY would need nearly all of the Bear's weight moved to the Bull. The price history matters as well. The shares slid through September and sit about a third below their $36.99 52-week high, and no source in the pack explains either move. On fixed scenarios, most closes on the page through September 9 sat more than 5.0% above our weighted fair value and would have derived SELL; every close from September 10 derives HOLD. The Base uses today's FY27E multiple, so it also inherits that slide. The label is sensitive to the price, and it is a HOLD at the September 29 close.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The pack's segment table shows a single consolidated line, but the 10-Q reports three operating segments; we follow the 10-Q. In Q2'26, Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products was 61% of revenue and 53% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, supplying canstock, closure stock, foilstock, Auto Body Sheet, heat exchanger materials and battery foil. Aerospace & Transportation was 25% of revenue and 44% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, supplying plate, sheet and extrusions to aerospace, space, transportation and defense customers. Automotive Structures & Industry was 17% of revenue and 8% of segment Adjusted EBITDA, making crash management systems, body structures and battery enclosure components plus extrusions and rail profiles. Holdings and Corporate was a 5% drag on Adjusted EBITDA. The revenue shares are as the 10-Q presents them and sum to more than the total, so we do not convert them into dollar figures. The mix makes aerospace the profit engine at a quarter of revenue.

moatFactors.name: Aerospace and defense products
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q describes many Aerospace & Transportation products as "mission critical" and its customers as "blue-chip" in aerospace, space and defense. It is the one segment whose share of segment Adjusted EBITDA exceeds its share of revenue, which is the evidence of an advantage. The pack has no data on contract terms or supplier qualification, so we do not claim more than that margin gap shows.

moatFactors.name: Metal pass-through and recycling
moatFactors.body: Products are priced on the LME price, a regional premium and a conversion margin, and the business model "aims to pass through" primary aluminum price exposure, hedging the rest where possible. Recycling lets the company buy scrap at a discount to primary metal. Both protect the conversion margin more than they widen it, and the 10-Q notes that a narrower scrap spread could have an unfavorable impact.

moatFactors.name: Secular demand trends
moatFactors.body: Management expects the vehicle lightweighting trend to continue and believes canstock has an attractive long-term growth outlook. These support demand over a cycle, but they are trends the whole industry shares rather than advantages specific to Constellium.

moatFactors.name: Competition and cyclicality
moatFactors.body: The 10-K says the company competes with producers "some of which are larger and have greater financial and technical resources", and that producers with a lower cost basis may have an advantage. Combined with the earnings swings in the income section, that limits pricing power outside aerospace.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow and sits mainly in aerospace. The aerospace and defense franchise shows a margin advantage the rest of the business lacks, and pass-through pricing and recycling steady the conversion margin. Packaging and automotive, which make up most of the revenue, are cyclical and competitive, and the company does not set the metal prices or premiums that drive its revenue. Durability therefore depends on aerospace growing into a larger share of profits; until it does, group returns will follow the cycle.

points: Aerospace: management says "aerospace demand has improved" and that destocking of aluminum products in the supply chain "continues to ease"; Aerospace & Transportation volumes rose 20% in the six months ended June 30, 2026.

Automotive: management expects the lightweighting trend to continue, but notes that vehicle sales fluctuate with the economic cycle, tariffs and affordability; Automotive Structures & Industry volumes fell 2% over the same six months.

Packaging: management says can demand has historically been "fairly resilient" through economic cycles, yet Packaging & Automotive Rolled Products volumes fell 3% over those six months, so growth there rests on the long-term outlook rather than current volumes.

Revenue: consensus is about $9 billion for both FY26E and FY27E, so the Street models no top-line growth after this year, and its EPS step-down points to lower profitability rather than lower revenue.
Group volume growth is concentrated in the segment that is a quarter of revenue; at group level, 2026 growth is mostly price.

management.leadership: Per the April 2026 proxy, Ingrid Joerg succeeded Jean-Marc Germain as Chief Executive Officer effective January 1, 2026; she was previously Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer and President of the Packaging, Automotive & Rolled Products business unit. Jack Guo is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Philippe Hoffmann is President of the Aerospace & Transportation business unit, and Ryan Jurkovic is Chief Human Resources Officer. Joerg's first two quarters as CEO produced strong results, but they coincided with metal prices well above the prior year's, so they say little yet about the new leadership's effect.
management.capitalAllocation: The company pays no dividend; cash goes to capital expenditure and buybacks. In FY25 it spent $330 million on capital expenditure and, per the proxy, returned $115 million through the repurchase of 8.9 million shares. In Q2'26 it returned $20 million through the repurchase of 623 thousand shares. Buybacks absorbed most of FY25's free cash flow, which is why net debt did not fall. We would rather see more of the surplus reduce debt while earnings are high: buying back stock in a year consensus expects to be followed by lower earnings leaves the debt in place for the downturn.
management.governance: The April 2026 proxy reports that, as of December 31, 2025, the board deemed Messrs. Blot, Brandjes, Deslarzes, Ormerod, Puig and Soultz and Mmes. Boccon-Gibod, Brooks and Walker independent under NYSE standards and the Board Charter. Ms. Joerg is not independent as CEO, and Mr. Verdier and Ms. Weiler are not independent as employees of the Company's subsidiaries. Nine independent directors against three who are not is a clear majority, which we read as adequate oversight for outside holders.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt carries no beneficial-ownership table, so the pack does not show insider holdings or whether any shareholder has significant influence.

idiosyncratic: Reversal of what lifted Q2'26: the North American auto-sheet shortages management credited may ease, and the 10-Q notes that a narrower scrap spread could have an unfavorable impact on results. Either would hit the conversion margin while revenue per ton falls with metal prices.
Leverage: the debt described in the balance section turns any earnings shortfall into a larger loss for shareholders, and it is the main reason our Bear is deep.
Competition: the 10-K warns that an existing or new competitor may add capacity, and that producers with a lower cost basis may have an advantage.

Substitution: the 10-K warns that higher aluminum prices relative to alternative materials may make aluminum products less competitive, a live risk with the average all-in U.S. aluminum price up 77% in Q2'26.
Leadership change: the CEO changed on January 1, 2026, and the new team has not yet run the business through a weaker market.
risks.systemic: Constellium's volumes follow the world economy: auto sales, air travel, consumer spending and industrial activity all feed demand, and the 10-Q notes that general economic conditions influence both volumes and prices. Trade policy is a direct exposure, since the 10-Q reports continued uncertainty related to tariffs and trade conditions. Energy is another: operations need substantial electricity and natural gas, and the company says the Middle East conflict has caused, and may continue to result in, higher fuel and energy prices. Currency moves create transaction and translation effects across its euro and dollar operations, and the 10-K lists interest rate fluctuations among its global risks. These forces tend to move together in a downturn, and the debt makes the equity more sensitive to them than the end-market mix alone would suggest.

body: We rate Constellium a HOLD with a $21 to $27 target range around a weighted fair value of $25.22. The aerospace franchise is growing and 2026 earnings are strong, but the price already reflects the FY27E consensus at today's multiple, and the debt makes the Bear deep. A reward/risk of 0.06x is far below the 0.50x a BUY needs.

On unchanged scenarios, a close below our target low would derive BUY, because reward/risk reaches the BUY threshold just above that level. SELL derives once the price sits more than 5.0% above our weighted fair value, which happens just inside our target high. We would move weight toward the Bull if FY27E consensus EPS rises toward the FY26E level, and toward the Bear if Aerospace & Transportation volume growth stops or net debt rises.
